drills.title: Initials from a messy name
drills.prompt: A signup form gives you a name with extra spaces. Arrange the lines so the program prints the initials. Two lines do not belong.
drills.explain: strip() removes the outer spaces, and split("\\s+") cuts on any run of spaces. A single-space split would leave empty pieces between the words and parts[1] would be "". substring(0, 1) is the first letter as a String, so it has toUpperCase(); charAt gives a plain char, which has no methods.

drills.title: Clean, find, cut and join
drills.prompt: Fill the blanks so the program prints the goal output.
drills.hint: Count the letters of Learning, or ask the text where the first space is.
drills.explain: strip() (or the older trim()) removes the outer spaces. indexOf gives the position of the first match, or -1 when there is none, while contains only says true or false. substring(0, 8) stops before index 8, so it keeps the 8 letters of Learning. String.join glues the pieces with the separator in front.

drills.title: New texts, old texts
drills.prompt: Read the code and type exactly what it prints, one line per line of output.
drills.explain: A String never changes: toUpperCase() returns a new text and line 2 throws it away, so s is still Java. substring(1, 4) takes indexes 1, 2 and 3 (the end is not included), substring(3) runs from index 3 to the end. indexOf answers -1 when the text is not found. split gives an array of 3 pieces, and length is its size.

drills.title: One step past the end
drills.prompt: The program should print the last digit of a card number, but it crashes while it runs. Click the line that crashes, then choose the fix.
code: System.out.println("Ends with " + last4 + ", last digit " + lastDigit);
fixed_code: System.out.println("Ends with " + last4 + ", last digit " + lastDigit);
drills.explain: Positions start at 0, so a text of 16 characters has indexes 0 to 15 and charAt(16) does not exist. The last character is always at length() - 1. Java has no negative indexes like card[-1] in Python, and length() needs its brackets for a String.

drills.title: Review the AI's signup check
drills.prompt: An AI assistant wrote this signup code. It compiles and runs, but tick the real problems (there are three).

issues.text: email.strip() does nothing: the cleaned text is never saved
issues.why: Strings cannot change. strip() returns a new String and the result is thrown away, so email still has its spaces. Write email = email.strip();

issues.text: plan == "pro" is false even though plan holds the letters pro, so Pro features never turn on
issues.why: == asks whether both sides are the very same object. A text built at run time (here by toLowerCase()) is a different object. Use plan.equals("pro").

issues.text: domain starts at the @, so it is @Gmail.com instead of Gmail.com
issues.why: substring(start) includes the character at start. Begin one position later: email.substring(email.indexOf("@") + 1).

non_issues.text: name.substring(0, 1) returns two letters because it goes from 0 to 1
non_issues.why: The end index is not included, so substring(0, 1) is only the character at index 0: A.

non_issues.text: indexOf("@") must be indexOf('@') because it looks for one character
non_issues.why: indexOf accepts both a String and a single char. Either works.

non_issues.text: The last line should use a StringBuilder instead of +
non_issues.why: StringBuilder pays off when you append many times in a loop. Joining three small pieces once with + is fine.

drills.explain: Three Day 4 rules hide in generated code: methods return new Strings, equals instead of ==, and substring(start) includes the start position. All three compile without a warning and fail quietly.
